text: Patrick McKenzie (patio11) is joined by returning guest Zvi Mowshowitz, AI watcher extraordinaire, to read Anthropic’s S-1 and what it shows about the AI industry. They cover a founder-controlled structure built on a single Class F share that holds 50.1% of the vote, an uncapped 3:1 employee donation match that may be the most expensive perk ever offered, and about $900 billion in forward compute commitments. They also discuss why softer Q3 revenue points to a shortage of GPUs rather than of customers, the bubble and circular-financing bear cases, and who should be blamed when AI-assisted hackers take $5 billion from Binance. Presenting Sponsor: Mercury Complex Systems is presented by Mercury. Mercury Payroll puts payroll, benefits, and compliance right inside your Mercury account. An in-house team backed by AI registers you in new states, files and remits your payroll taxes, and handles the notices, so you don’t have to copy from PDFs to Excel to web portals. Setup takes minutes, and Mercury Payroll is free for eligible Mercury customers through the end of 2026 at mercury.com/payroll Timestamps: (00:00) Intro (01:35) How the S-1 talks about existential risk (07:45) Anthropic has long had an attitude (12:20) Anthropic’s uncapped donation matching (14:18) Postscript: what the matching program will actually cost (16:00) Sponsor: Mercury (18:29) Revenue growth and cohort economics (22:25) Postscript: Q3 was a supply story, not a demand story (24:55) Is it a bubble? (28:27) Sizing the market for tokens (31:02) The commodification bear case (31:56) Cash efficiency and $800 billion in compute commitments (36:44) Postscript: what happens if the commits go bad (39:20) Flexing compute between training, inference and subleasing (43:37) Reading an S-1, with and without an LLM (46:49) Circular financing and the dot-com comparison (50:08) Wall Street versus the tech industry (52:02) The three AI pills (54:53) Industrial revolutions and how weird the future gets (57:31) AI mathematics and the bitter lesson (01:00:52) Capabilities nobody trained for (01:04:40) Capabilities versus diffusion (01:07:12) Token spend at the frontier (01:09:09) Final thoughts on the S-1 (01:11:48) The hackening and who bears responsibility (01:17:49) Trapdoors and irreversible decisions (01:19:12) Wrap Patrick: Welcome to Complex Systems, where we discuss the technical, organizational, and human factors underpinning why the world works the way it does. Hideho, everyone. My name is Patrick McKenzie, better known as patio11 on the internet. I'm here with multi-time guest Zvi Mowshowitz . Thanks very much for coming on. Zvi: Glad to be back. Yeah, I always enjoy it. Patrick: So we're discussing the Anthropic S-1 today, and the larger window that it shares on the AI industry. And because we are professionals discussing professionally adjacent topics, we have to start with the boring parts, similar to the boring disclaimers in an S-1. I don't believe I own stock in any of the labs. I don't invest in publicly traded tech stocks except through ETFs that are broadly market-tracking. [ Patrick notes : You don’t come to me for investment advice, and that is a good thing, because this has been a really poor decision for the 20+ years I’ve been in tech.] I have a career in the tech industry, which is getting drawn into the gravitational well of the labs right now and the other parts of the AI supply chain, and you should assume I'm conflicted up the wazoo in that fashion. But I think I'm trying to be a reasonably responsible person talking about this company, and I think that's all for me. [ Patrick notes : To be slightly more explicit: I am socially connected to many people at the labs, including former coworkers and bosses, a few of whom are now quite senior. Both major American labs have had commercial discussions with me. Other non-lab companies in the AI industry have paid me substantial amounts of money for consulting and, separately, advertising spots on Complex Systems. You may reasonably model these and similar relationships recurring in the future. I believe that Stripe equity, which I own through having worked there, and which is the supermajority of my family’s assets, is materially exposed to the AI industry both mechanically and via investor sentiment.] Do you want to add any for yourself? Zvi: I do buy individual stocks. I own Google and Amazon, relevant to Anthropic, but I deliberately did not invest directly in Anthropic because of potential conflict of interest concerns. Patrick: And nothing that you hear on this podcast is investment advice. Okay. So let's start it out. You recently wrote something of your own perspective on the S-1, which had some key takeaways. Do you want to walk people through those key takeaways? Zvi: Yeah. So as usual, when I look at anything from Anthropic, I want to see their attitude towards existential risk, alignment, whether or not they're going to potentially kill everyone. So in this case, they mention existential risk only in passing, only in the passive voice. They're clearly trying to have it both ways. When they talk to the investors, they want to say, "Oh, look at our big mission, but our big mission is to build this super profitable hypercomputing thing." And then other times they want to say, "Our geniuses in the data center actually might kill everyone," and these two things have to coexist. Similarly, pacing the frontier is something they do talk about here, but then they make clear to investors, "Don't worry. When we said pacing the frontier, we did not mean not making incredibly fast AI progress. We did not mean voluntarily let someone else go first. We just meant it would be great if everybody could collectively agree to go only at super speed and not at ludicrous speed." But they will do the embedded evaluations. Similarly, we're all worried about recursive self-improvement. And here they call that "closing the loop" to be more business-friendly, but they say that their entire business model is they want to close the loop. They are worried that if someone else closes the loop before they close the loop, they will be out of the loop and they will lose. So they intend to close the loop as fast as possible and as much as possible. Patrick: I feel like there is an interesting tension around S-1s, because we largely have this culture in the tech industry of, necessarily, Zuck speaks for Facebook and Facebook speaks for Zuck. Tech has done complicated innovations with share classes that enable the founder/company relationship to be relatively durable over a period of years and decades. [ Patrick notes : Facebook was not the first company to issue super-voting founder shares but it popularized the model. Pattern matching goes both ways with Silicon Valley investors: you should believe your new investment is the second coming of Facebook. If you don’t, stop now; returns in venture are heavily weighted towards a handful of generational companies, and the entire game is spreading out your fund such that you are definitely in them and persuading the founder that you will be easy to work with (and so please don’t cut your allocation in any round). If you believe you are investing in the next Facebook, you affirmatively want the next Zuck at the helm durably regardless of how diluted their economic stake gets as they raise capital. Public market investors, seeing a company which grew from a dorm room to a global power, largely seem to accept precedent on provisions guaranteeing founder control. If founders have them at IPO, they keep them.] Patrick continues : Founder-led companies are something of a thing, and Anthropic is doing its own thing with respect to complicated share classes, which we can get into in a minute, if people are very interested in the mechanics of single shares that have more than 50% of the voting power, yada, yada, yada. But when you get the quote-unquote "responsible adults" in the room — S-1s are largely drafted by external counsel and counsel working for the banks that are the underwriters of the S-1. Responsible adults say: "We all understand that everyone in the tech industry thinks that the CEO runs the company. However, managerial capitalism says that the CEO only runs the company to the extent that they're not fired by the board on behalf of the shareholders. And while you've taken some amount of effort to make sure that that never happens, we have to pretend that in principle it is possible that it happens, and so we can't privilege the CEO's voice among many other voices." And there's a difference between when the CEO is stating their own opinion in their own spaces and when they're speaking on behalf of the company, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. And I think in some parts, there is the usual level of cynicism that prevails in corporate communications, and in some parts authors sincerely believe, "No, there is a ritual here. We deeply buy into the ritual, and we care about the boundaries of it." But there has been much mirth around the use of passive voice in talking about the AI risks to humanity, because "concerns have been raised" is an understatement, as has been pointed out by yourself and Matt Levine and many others. The “concerns” call was coming from inside the house, at the executive level and essentially all other levels of Anthropic. So it is an interesting inversion of the normal form, where the normal form is not claiming that the company could potentially kill everyone, and that would be bad for business results. Zvi: Yeah, I mean, obviously it's a compromise between — the bankers would rather not mention this at all, because if everyone is killed, you will not in fact be sued for securities fraud. There will be no one left to sue you. And Dario and others at the company presumably wanted to use not only the passive voice but the active voice, and be much louder and more extensive about it, and use it as an opportunity. Patrick: And there's also liability-minimization happening here, where lawyers will always advise you, "Don't say anything that you don't need to say. Anything that you don't need to say to get the transaction, deal, testimony, et cetera done just creates risk needlessly." And so if you feel emotionally or aesthetically or morally committed to saying, "No, we could kill everyone," the lawyers will say, reasonably, "Well, when you say that, you're providing causes of action to people in the future for any of a variety of things that could happen, including nothing much different than what is happening in the status quo.” [ Patrick notes : I believe this factor is underrated. Consider a very prosaic lawsuit about an ordinary corporate matter. If the opposed side wants to demonstrate cavalier recklessness, which is frequently good legal strategy, one way to demonstrate recklessness is contrasting testimony that all normal steps were taken with “Really? Because at your firm, doing things that might end humanity is a normal Tuesday . Do you recall the following language from your S-1/senior executives/company culture guide/etc.”] The lawyer will continue: “And that will be quoted against you, and it will be worse for being quoted against you from an S-1 versus from a blog post, because the various people that look at these things, like regulators in Washington, DC generally and potentially courts in the future, care about things in an S-1 much more than they care about things that are in a blog post. And we will be able to wave away things that are in the blog post in the future as, 'Oh, that was just his opinion,' et cetera, et cetera. But we can't really wave away things in the S-1.” Zvi: Right. And from my perspective, the whole idea is, everything in terms of the financial incentive — the lawyers, the corporation people, the lobbyists, the PR guy, the usual suspects, all the business interests — will in fact want to downplay and ignore and sweep aside, and make everybody else sweep away and ignore, all of these concerns. And my view essentially is that if we do too much of that, there's a very good chance that in fact AI will kill everyone, either from Anthropic or otherwise. And the argument that, "Oh no, this is the place where we have to say it in a way that matters, therefore we shouldn't say it the way that you want to say it" — well, I say that's exactly my reason why you should say it there, and why, if you choose not to make a costly signal, you've told me who you are. You've told me you're not willing to make a sacrifice that's meaningful. You are signaling to me that, in fact, you will prioritize other considerations higher. You just did so. That's the whole point of the exercise. And I understand entirely why people would choose to prioritize messaging to other people in these situations, but I never treat it as an excuse or as a reason to not care in the other directions. Should you choose these other considerations over the considerations that I care about — and maybe I even think you're right to do so—I'm going to knock you for having done it. Patrick: Cool. Shall we go to the second part of your takeaways, which was on control, I think? Zvi: Anthropic has long had an attitude, like many tech companies, as you point out, that the founders should continue to control the company, and that the worst thing that could happen to Anthropic would be to have the likes of Google and Amazon suddenly having them maximize shareholder value and then thinking about only corporate things. And then their company would probably go out there and increase the risk that the world is destroyed, and lose their unique company culture, and this would be extremely bad. So to that end, Anthropic has a very weird structure that they made even weirder in advance of the IPO. They have the one Class F share that belongs to the founders, and the founders collectively vote on how to exercise that share. And that share has 50.1% of the voting power for a wide range of issues, which is another way of saying the founders will keep control of the company as long as at least three of the founders continue to show up to the company, which could last quite a long time. Anthropic's anticipation is this will last until long after the fate of the world has been decided one way or another. And this seems rather likely, because there are something like nine of them, and only three of them have to keep showing up. Patrick adds post-interview: patio11 here with a brief correction of the record. So formally, Anthropic has seven founders, and there is an additional sort of early employee who gets a footnote, Benjamin Mann, but he is not formally one of the founders and doesn't get this inclusion into the Class F share class. Also, by the way, Zvi says at one point that it's Class H that might side with the founders. The employees that donate equity to charity are getting Class E voting rights rather than Class H voting rights. Okay, back to the flow. Zvi: And similarly, they have set up a Long-Term Benefit Trust, which will appoint nominally four of the seven board members over the long term, which in theory would've given them control of the company. But if you look at the actual details, the board appoints three, the Long-Term Benefit Trust appoints three, and then there's the seventh seat, which is suggested by the Long-Term Benefit Trust, but has to be effectively approved by the founders. And if the founders don't agree, then it goes to the vote of the employees who donated stock to charity, also known as the Class E shares. And a default assumption would be that the Class E shares would side with the founders. Patrick: I don't think I've ever heard of another company explicitly privileging employees with share classes. Generally, it's something of the reverse. [ Patrick notes : Employees most typically get stock options or restricted stock units which are designed to convert into common stock, or into a second class of common that is economically identical and differs only in voting, with the distinction typically disappearing after IPO or sale. Companies sometimes offer employees inducements to impair their stock in some way, such as accepting a voting proxy agreement (ceding their votes to the founders) in return for e.g. better-than-market exercise terms for their options. Common shares vote like Republicans in Chicago: mathematically you have no say in outcomes, but you do have a right to have your opinion tallied.] And it's interesting. It says you believe something strongly about your alignment, in the non-central sense of the word for AI, in that you have successfully recruited multiple cohorts of people who — The traditional thing to do in the tech industry is to have the employees proxy their votes to the founders, and the founders literally get to vote them in whichever way they want. And you're, in doing this, suggesting, "No, I think the employees are sufficiently philosophically aligned with management that they will proxy without a proxy agreement being in place," which is an interesting point of view. And I'm not saying "interesting" as a way of saying I don't think it is well-calibrated. In my many conversations with various people at Anthropic, they do seem to be quote-unquote "more aligned" than one would suggest for most tech companies at that stage, with that employee count, at that revenue growth rate, et cetera, et cetera. [ Patrick notes : Many companies experience, after hypergrowth, discontent among long-time employees (and sometimes founders) that the company has lost something special in the culture. Sometimes this is diagnosed as “we got lame and the cool people left.” I think it is more similar to reversion to the mean: you had a core of N people, distinguished in some way. You then intentionally, as a mechanical consequence of hypergrowth and with your eyes open, hired 10 people with impeccable credentials from AppAmaGooBookSoft for every one who previously worked with you. You will always find your culture drawn to the median culture of AppAmaGooBookSoft as a result of this choice. You will be warned about it in advance, and you will say “It will not happen here!” It will happen to you. It happened to AppAmaGooBookSoft, too.] Patrick continues : Not that there is another company at that revenue growth rate to point to, but we will get to that in a moment, I think. Zvi: Well, so before we move on, I would say Anthropic has long cultivated a very special company culture that has a large awareness of safety, but also of altruistic goals and charity and making the world a better place. The founders have famously pledged 80% of their shares to charity, and they've offered very, very generous matching donations for those who want to give their stock away. And in fact, how much stock you gave away determines how many Class E shares you have to vote. So they're, on several levels, determining, no, these are the preselected people who have very, very costly signaled that they want to influence the future in generally good ways, rather than build personal wealth and maximize profits. Those are the people who will ultimately make the tie-breaking vote in this situation, and that is exactly what that was selected for. Patrick: I couldn't find if this was explicitly called out in the S-1, and I will edit the transcript if I missed it in my first two readings. But their matching program for employees might be one of the most expensive single corporate decisions ever made in the history of capitalism. The matching program for employees was, I hear, calibrated to essentially allow employees to do something similar to what the founders were doing, and give away 80% of their economic stake. And to make those numbers work, they said that the corporation will basically match employee donations on a 3:1 basis, which is unheard of in the rest of capitalism. And additionally, typically a corporate matching program is: okay, we will match on a one-to-one basis up to, let's say, $7,000 a year. And so you say, okay, well, optimally executed, that option is worth $7,000 to charity, and perhaps $10,000, $11,000 or so in pre-tax income. The Anthropic matching program is uncapped. And so there are employees that will donate $20 million to charity and have it get backed by $60 million of Anthropic money in the wake of the IPO and their continued operation and similar. And when you sum that over extremely charitably minded employees, times thousands of them, times many of them that have presumptively eight- and nine-figure equity values, which they will quickly be giving away, that is just going to be an extremely expensive decision. Zvi: Yeah, but they got what they wanted out of it. You want to strongly differentiate yourself as an employer and attract aligned employees. If you're not committed to the mission, it sounds expensive, but if you are mission-aligned, the expense is a positive. And when you turn out to be the fastest-growing company in history, and the stock is worth close to $2 trillion, it will be a larger line item than you thought. But at the same time, you'll be able to afford it conditional on success, so it works both ways. Patrick injects via new recording: I failed at Ctrl+F prior to recording. The S-1 does indeed mention the donation matching program in a few places. For example, it says that the Class N shares are reserved against the need to make good on these commitments, and the company took a $2 billion non-cash charge in Q3 related to it. So in terms of cash, the matching program will be close to free. Shareholders as a class, inclusive of donors, pay for it through dilution. In terms of accounting, though, when you promise people compensation worth billions of dollars, we want to record the fact that you have promised billions of dollars. When you promise them compensation based on future world states, we update the cost of that promise as we learn more about the future. I suspect the Q3 charge is very far from the last non-cash charge attributable to the matching program. Future charges will happen as employees make new pledges, as past pledges not yet settled get remarked from a 409A valuation to the public price, and, probably the dominant factor, as currently pledged equity continues to vest and gets matched at public market prices rather than the private ones. The S-1 suggests there is presently about $24 billion in unvested equity compensation, with that calculation being made as of the day the equity was granted . When the cost of the match is calculated, it is calculated the day the equity vests , which will probably be at a higher valuation. And then you assume that much of the equity is going to employees eligible for three-to-one matching at the new mark, and much of the remainder to employees eligible for one-to-one matching at the new mark, and that probably tens of percent of it will be donated. And so, yep, that is almost certainly the most expensive perk in the history of capitalism. I suspect the magnitude of the first post-IPO charges is going to surprise people. Much has been written, including by my former colleague Nan, of the coming tidal wave of charitable donations . A large portion of that tidal wave flows through Anthropic's P&L. Zvi: So the next section of questions is about money, of course. So Anthropic is one of the fastest-growing companies in history. We're talking about 10x year over year for several years in a row. We're talking, in some places, even greater than that. First two quarters this year were completely nuts. Patrick: About 15x in the first half, right? [ Patrick notes : $1.16 billion in H1 2025 to $16.3 billion in H1 2026, so about 14x, though what is one entire prior-year half between friends.] Zvi: Right. Approximately, something like that, 15x in the first half, from a very large baseline to begin with, rather than from very small amounts. I mean, in the beginning it was like, okay, you're 10x-ing, but this is not unheard of because it's a very small company. Now it's a relatively large company, and people are asking questions like, how many times can you 10x? The entire economy is only so big. There are only so many Fortune 500 companies. It's just 500. At some point you're going to run out of targets. But that's not necessarily something we're getting close to. Quarter three, they did slow their growth. So their growth was still the envy of almost every company on Earth, but by their own standards, it was reasonably small. We have a variety of explanations for this. Anthropic was relatively badly positioned in terms of the quality of their available models and their appeal to business, compared to how they had been in the previous period or in the later period that we're in now. So that's probably my guess as to the main reason. There's also some talk about quarter three just being a slow period for growth, relatively speaking, due to the calendar. But my expectation is that quarter three was relatively slow, but that quarter four has picked up again, and you will see some very, very large growth numbers out of Anthropic. Patrick: In analysis of securities, we have to pretend that the gross quarter-to-quarter revenue results matter. But in this case, I think Anthropic is properly modeled more or less as a software company, where what you are doing is stacking cohorts together. And for reasons, we do not require software companies to break out their cohort numbers in S-1s and similar. [ Patrick notes : This is extremely well-understood among the best managers in the world, and relatively well-understood among investors. One classic articulation of it is Bezos’ in 2017 , referencing a much slower-moving business which was once the fastest growing business of all time: “Those quarterly results were fully baked three years ago. So today I'm working on a quarter that will happen in 2020, not next quarter. Next quarter is done already and it's probably been done for a couple years.”] If we did, that would be a fascinating window into the growth of the business. And so the cohorts are often heterogeneous with each other, and so the customers that you recruited in Q3 2026 are at a different point in their ramp of spend than the customers you recruited in Q3 2025, than in 2024. And the very interesting thing that you would want to see on those graphs is: do they asymptote at any point? And finger to the wind, my guess is the answer is no. The S-1 says they have a net revenue retention of 900%, which is silly for any other SaaS business. If you were doing 110%, that would be wonderful. [ Patrick notes : Slight exaggeration; that’s workmanlike execution for an IPOable SaaS company selling on annual contracts.] But my guess is their "early adopter customers," the ones that were there in the ancient history of two years ago, have not figured the limits of cognition in their businesses yet, and are continuing to pour money at tokens and get business results out. And if you were hypothetically in a world where a cohort graph would show that, okay, after the first two years of adoption, the growth pace goes to that of a normal software business, then you would be much more bearish on Anthropic and labs generally as a business. I suspect we are not in that world. I suspect the line for people that have been on two years continues to be vertical, and it will look less vertical in the first three months of a customer's life, as they do things like internal pilots, IT starts to get involved, yada, yada, yada, all that fun stuff for the absorption of this technology in the world. And so I suspect quarter-to-quarter softness in the number is more an artifact of how the cohort graphs stack up than it is an artifact of the total corporate positioning relative to competitors in that quarter. But I do not have internal numbers on this. Obviously, if I had internal numbers, I would not be able to share them. Patrick: After recording the episode, I thought through this a bit more, including with Claude assisting, and have a better hypothesis. As I mentioned, it is useful to have lenses available, like being a SaaS-y guy, because it lets you see the world in terms of cohorts. It sometimes impairs your vision, though, because you imagine every business as having arbitrarily high margins and the ability to scale to customer demand as quickly as DevOps can type into their terminal. Anthropic is, importantly, less like a software business in those respects. Anthropic says in the S-1, "We have historically operated in a compute-constrained environment in which demand for compute has exceeded the supply available to us." Their ability to service revenue from fully bought-in customers is limited by the contracted, racked, powered GPUs available to them. The S-1 says historically they make these arrangements 12 to 18 months in advance. And so, in roughly Q1 or Q2 of 2025, they had to make a guess as to how compute efficient a yet-to-be-released Opus 5.5 would be, and how much customers would be willing to use it. Anthropic seems to have underestimated or —in Zvi's parlance elsewhere—perhaps simply not to have been aggressive enough. Their Q3 revenue softening isn't a demand story. It's a supply story. They're running all the GPUs they have, and it just isn't enough. Supporting evidence: they talk about hitting the spot market for GPUs for $5 billion, at substantially more than their multi-year commitments typically run, in such a way as to eat 10% of the margin just from the shift in the mix. You'd assume low tens of percent of revenue is served by spot compute, but that spot compute made up 50% of their compute spend for the quarter. The S-1 says "short-term commitments," which might not line up one-to-one with, for example, how AWS will sell you a spot instance. Roll with me here on the lingo. The important bit is that you're paying through the nose for availability as a trade-off for not contracting for that capacity in advance. And so why has the revenue softened? Either because you want to make the principled decision that you don't want to climb the cost curve in the spot market and sell at wafer-thin margins or for a loss just to inflate your top-line metrics, or perhaps because you just tapped all the spot that capitalism had available in Q3 2026. I think analysts who read this as softening demand would need to explain tapping spot for 50% of one's spend. I frankly don't think there is an explanation available there. These analysts are just straightforwardly wrong. Even if one allocates all of the spot compute to training runs for Opus 6.x or whatever, that's still saying they fully saturated the long-term contracted chips, and their customers still had tokens waiting. Zvi: Yep, it's really hard to say. There's a lot of different factors. We have very low visibility, for a variety of obvious reasons. We have to endlessly hear the same people predict the imminent fall of OpenAI and Anthropic, and the imminent commodification of the models, and the imminent — everybody's going to stop spending so much on tokens. And they say this every time the number 10xes, which has been a remarkably large number of times. And yes, at some point, number has gone up, and estimates of the future rate of number going up will go down, and therefore stock price will go down even as the token usage and the revenue numbers go up. And at that point, people will talk about the bubble bursting, and they will be wrong. That is the default. Obviously, nothing I say is investment advice. As per usual, nothing you say is investment advice. But it's very easy to predict who will continuously predict these things happening and who will not. Patrick: I think reasonably well-calibrated people could think, just on priors: I'm not paying much attention to what AI is doing. I've just heard this story before. "This time is different" as a meme. This feels in some ways like the classic examples from Byrne Hobart and Tobias Huber's book, Boom , where when a new input for industry gets developed. We overshoot the actual demand for it for a couple of years. We dump hundreds of billions of dollars or more into investment that is initially unproductive. The early investors get shellacked at some point. Then, there is a period of wandering in the wilderness, and then we eventually figure out how to use all the infrastructure investment that we made. Zvi: Yeah, there are so many differences with that model that exist here. One of which is that the initial investment is not initially idle or useless. There is actually overwhelming demand for everything that you can get right now, while the systems get clearly better at a very rapid pace. So even if you're not going to talk about AGI or superintelligence or all the things that we're going to do in a couple of years, this just seems transparently very different to me. Patrick: Yep. Not to kick crypto while it's down — by the way, breaking news from the day before we recorded this: Binance was hacked for somewhere north of $5 billion , likely in a way that was accelerated by AI by North Korea. [ Patrick notes : This podcast was recorded immediately after the attack; Binance claims that partners successfully froze or intercepted approximately $2.85 billion of $6.34 billion taken. One should expect that number to evolve over time. Either way, North Korea’s Lazarus Group has stolen the crown for the largest robbery in history from… themselves. Their previous high-water mark was the $1.5 billion stolen from Bybit in 2025 .] At any rate, crypto boosters consistently said, for 15 years, "Next year is going to be the year of mass institutional adoption." [ Patrick notes : They have a reasonable argument that stablecoins for B2B payments are a scaled, novel, non-speculative use case for crypto. They also confidently said that Bitcoin would be used for payments because its security and fees were superior to banks’ offerings, that securities would move to blockchains out of technological superiority and to decrease counterparty risk, that NFTs would lead to a new flourishing of the arts, that novel VMs running on top of blockchains would be the primary application development platform for the financial industry, etc. And crypto advocates made a lot of money investing early and convincing others to buy them out of those investments using those claims, which makes them retrospectively effective claims if not true claims, to a certain strain of logic.] And AI is like, "Well, no, this year is the year of mass institutional adoption, except next year we will 10x this number." A billion dollars in revenue going to $16 billion in revenue, going to who knows what it'll be next year, for a part-year period, is just wild. So I think I'm with you. I think folks that are doing the "this is just a bubble because it pattern-matches to every other bubble" thing. As dangerous as it is to say "this time it is actually different," the actual object-level reality matters . This time is indeed discontinuously different compared to other bubbles we have seen in our lifetimes and historical examples. [ Patrick notes : “This time is different” is a phrase which notoriously ages poorly after it is said during bubble conditions. “This time is actually different” ages even more poorly.
